name: Zina Kotoko
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Odden, David. 2005. The Unnatural Tonology of Zina Kotoko. Ms., Ohio State University, dated 21 Feb 2005, 'Submitted to the Procedings of the TIE Conference, Santorini'; 20 pp. Published 2007 in T. Riad & C. Gussenhoven (eds.), Tones and Tunes, Vol. 1: Typological Studies in Word and Sentence Prosody, 63-90. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter (doi:10.1515/9783110207569.63). Internet Archive copy of the author's former OSU page:https://web.archive.org/web/2016id_/http://ling.ohio-state.edu/~odden/Unnatural%20Tonology%20of%20Kotoko.pdf
catalog_locator: p. 8 of the 2005 preprint, section 4 'Consonant-Tone Effects in Zina Kotoko', first paragraph.
catalog_quote: The language has three distinctive tones: L marked with a grave accent, H marked with acute accent, and M which is unmarked. Lexical tone is contrastive in nouns but not in verbs, which receive surface tones in a predictable manner based on an interaction between suffixal tones or floating tones indicating tense-aspect, and phonological rules which include consonantally-conditioned tone lowerings. There are a number of distinct tone lowering rules in the grammar which refer to different classes of consonants.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Zina Kotoko is a three-tone language (L, M, H); tone is lexically contrastive on nouns and grammatically assigned on verbs. The source says nothing about word stress or accent, so no stress position can be stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant to stress; the paper is about consonant-conditioned tone lowering (voiced obstruents, sonorants, glottal stop and implosives as depressors).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone; data are single-consultant elicitations (Habi, Tromsø field-methods class 1999-2000); citation forms are verb inflections and nouns.
new_statements.identity_note: Odden's 'Zina Kotoko' = Glottolog Jina (jina1244, ISO jia), Kotoko South group of Central Chadic; Odden's data come from a single consultant (Habi) in a 1999-2000 Tromsø field-methods class, Tourneux's from Oumar Adam (Maroua 1989, 1997, 2003). Tourneux (2005, p. 2) says the language is spoken only in Cameroonian villages (Zina, Cεlεy, Sasara, Gεdεba, Marawma, Gεlεy; ~2,000 speakers), though Glottolog lists Cameroon and Chad. Odden's 2005 ms calls Afade, Lagwan, Mser, Mpade, Maslam, Malgbe and Mazera 'dialects' of Kotoko; Gravina 2014 treats them as separate languages, with Zina and Mazera forming Kotoko South.

tone_statements.citation: Odden, David. 2002. Consonant-Tone Interaction in Zina Kotoko. Stanford Linguistics Colloquium, Stanford University, 19 April 2002 (talk abstract).
tone_statements.quote: This paper describes verbal tone in the Chadic language Zina Kotoko, spoken in northern Cameroun. Kotoko is relevant to the study of consonant-tone interaction because the entire system of tone assignment in verbs is based on interaction between tense-aspect and the consonants in the stem: there are no lexical tone properties in verb roots. [...] First, most languages with such effects are 2-tone-level languages: Kotoko lowers M to L and H to M, indicating at least that "lowering by one step" is a possible tone-depressor strategy for three-level languages.
tone_statements.locator: colloquium abstract (single HTML page), paragraphs 1 and 4

tone_statements.citation: Odden, David. n.d. [c. 2000; PDF created 19 March 2010]. Kotoko after 3 weeks. Unpublished field-methods sample paper (University of Tromsø field methods class 1999-2000, Zina Kotoko consultant), posted on Odden's Ohio State University Linguistics 650 course page (www.ling.ohio-state.edu/~odden/650/). 8 pp. (§1 Consonants, §2 Vowels, §3 Prosody). the Internet Archive capture of 10 July 2010.
tone_statements.quote: Vowel length does not appear to be contrastive in the language. However, the language does have distinctive tones. Tonal distinctions are at present not very clear, but there seem to be three tone levels: H, M and L. No contour tones have been observed so far. The phonetic distinction between L and M tones is small, in contrast to M and H which seem to be separated by a larger step. Tonal values should at present be taken to be very tenative. Monosyllabic nouns are rare, but H and L (not M) are attested in monosyllabic nouns.

sources.quote: This paper describes verbal tone in the Chadic language Zina Kotoko, spoken in northern Cameroun. Kotoko is relevant to the study of consonant-tone interaction because the entire system of tone assignment in verbs is based on interaction between tense-aspect and the consonants in the stem: there are no lexical tone properties in verb roots. [...] First, most languages with such effects are 2-tone-level languages: Kotoko lowers M to L and H to M, indicating at least that "lowering by one step" is a possible tone-depressor strategy for three-level languages.
sources.locator: colloquium abstract (single HTML page), paragraphs 1 and 4
sources.note: Abstract read in full: Zina Kotoko has three tone levels (H, M, L); verb roots have no lexical tone, verbal tone is assigned by floating tense-aspect tones (M past, H habitual, MH imperative) plus three consonant-conditioned lowering rules (H-Lowering H->M after voiced obstruents/sonorants/glottal stop; M-Lowering M->L also after implosives; Pre-Depressor Lowering M->L before a voiced obstruent); glottal stop and implosives act as depressors.
